entry.title: SightPress 0.4.0: themes you can choose and media without limits
entry.summary: SightPress 0.4.0 lets you choose a theme for each site and change its colours, and handles large files, captions, transcripts and cloud storage.
entry.content:
SightPress 0.4.0 is out. It's about two things: how your website looks, and the pictures, videos and recordings you put on it. You can now choose a theme for each site and change its colours, and SightPress handles large files, captions, transcripts and cloud storage.

What's new

#Link to this section: What's new

Choose a theme for each site

#Link to this section: Choose a theme for each site

A new Appearance screen lists every installed theme, with its status in words and a picture of the theme with a description. If there's no picture, the screen describes the theme in words. Preview opens a sample page with every kind of block in that theme, so you can look before you change anything. Each site can use its own theme, and your pages and their content stay the same when you change it.

Themes are installed on the server by whoever runs SightPress, never uploaded through the website. That keeps your site safe.

Change the colours, but never lose contrast

#Link to this section: Change the colours, but never lose contrast

You can change a theme's colours for light and dark mode. SightPress checks every pair of colours that appear together. If a colour would be too hard to read, it's refused, and the message names the colours that clash and their contrast. What you typed is kept, so you can adjust it. Every theme goes through the same checks before it can be installed, and again before it's applied.

The admin panel keeps its own colours whatever you choose, so you can always find your way around.

More page layouts

#Link to this section: More page layouts

Besides the home page and standard layouts, pages can now use a landing layout, a sidebar layout that lists the other pages in the same section, and a full width layout for wide galleries and tables. On a narrow screen or when zoomed in, every layout becomes a single column. If you switch to a theme that lacks a layout, SightPress lists the pages affected before anything changes.

Make your own theme

#Link to this section: Make your own theme

Developers can start a new theme from the theme template. It comes with the checks, the tests and a step-by-step tutorial, and the checks explain in words what needs fixing.

Captions and transcripts

#Link to this section: Captions and transcripts

Videos can now have captions in each of your site's languages. SightPress checks each captions file and tells you which line to fix. Videos and recordings get a transcript that visitors open with a button under the player. A page with a video or recording can't be published until it has them.

If the AI assistant is on, it can add punctuation, paragraphs and speaker labels to a transcript. It can't change the words, and a person still checks the result against the recording before the page can be published.

Upload large files, and carry on if they stop

#Link to this section: Upload large files, and carry on if they stop

Large files are now sent in small parts, with a progress bar that screen readers announce every 10%. You can pause, resume or cancel an upload. If your connection drops, or you close the page, you can carry on from where the upload stopped for up to a day. Each site can also have its own upload limits, and files too large for the browser can be imported from the server, with the same safety checks.

Keep your files in the cloud, if you want to

#Link to this section: Keep your files in the cloud, if you want to

A site can keep its files in cloud storage such as AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2, and let a content delivery network (CDN) send public files from near each visitor. Unpublished files and every file of a members-only site stay protected: their addresses stop working after a short time, so a shared link doesn't give them away. SightPress can set everything up at AWS or Cloudflare, and moves your files safely, checking each one.

All of this is optional. By default your files stay on your own server, and nothing goes to another company unless you choose to set it up. When you do, SightPress picks a location that matches the site's country: London for UK sites, and the EU for sites in Europe.

What it isn't yet

#Link to this section: What it isn't yet

SightPress is still an early release for trying out and testing, and running it on a public server isn't covered yet. The next release is about extending SightPress: modules from other developers, custom roles and optional text messages.

Try it

#Link to this section: Try it

The SightPress documentation has new guides to changing a theme, choosing page layouts, adding captions and transcripts, uploading large files and keeping files in the cloud. There's also a tutorial for creating your own theme. The 0.4.0 release notes list every change.

If you design themes, or you rely on captions and transcripts, I'd love to hear how this release works for you.

entry.title: AI is what we make of it
entry.summary: AI isn't a monster or a miracle, it's a tool. A blind developer on what AI does well, what it does badly, and how we should use it.
entry.content:
Artificial intelligence isn't a monster and it isn't a miracle. It's a tool. Used with care, it does real good. Used carelessly, it does real harm. Which of those we get depends on people, not on the machine.

This is an opinion piece, and I'm not neutral. I'm a blind developer, I use AI every working day, and I think the people who could gain most from it are too often told to keep away. I'll set out what AI does well, what it does badly, and the rules I think we should all use it by.

We have been here before

#Link to this section: We have been here before

Every important technology arrived with a wave of fear. People worried that the printing press would spread lies, that electricity would burn down cities, that the telephone would end real conversation and that the internet would rot our minds. Some of those fears were partly right. Printed lies did spread. The internet does have its dark corners.

But nobody sensible argues today that we should have stopped printing books or switched off the web. We learned, slowly and imperfectly, to use them well. We wrote laws, built habits and set expectations. The technology didn't decide the outcome. We did.

AI is the same. The question isn't whether it's good or bad. The question is how we choose to use it.

What AI does well

#Link to this section: What AI does well

The everyday benefit of AI isn't dramatic, and that's exactly why it matters. It takes the tiring, repetitive part out of ordinary work.

  • It finds things. A researcher can search a mountain of papers and find the five that matter.
  • It translates. A small charity with no budget for a translator can offer its pages in a second language.
  • It explains. A developer can ask what an unfamiliar library does instead of spending an afternoon on forums.
  • It summarises. A writer can get the gist of a long report and decide whether it's worth reading in full.
  • It describes. It can tell someone who can't see what's in a photo, a chart or a screen.

None of this replaces thinking. It removes friction, so people have more time and energy to think. That's what good tools have always done.

What AI does badly

#Link to this section: What AI does badly

I'd be a poor advocate if I only told you the good parts. AI has real weaknesses, and anyone who uses it should know them.

  • It's confidently wrong. AI can invent a fact, a quote or a source and present it in exactly the same calm tone as the truth. It can describe a photo of a cat as a dog. It doesn't know when it doesn't know.
  • It can be biased. It learns from what people have written, and it repeats their blind spots: about disability, about gender, about which languages and places matter.
  • It makes deception cheap. Spam, fake reviews, cloned voices and fake photos are now easy for anyone to produce, in bulk.
  • It can leak what you give it. Whatever you paste in leaves your hands. A document full of other people's personal details isn't yours to send to a stranger's server.
  • It raises fair questions about where it came from. Writers and artists have good reason to ask whether their work was used to build these tools without their permission, and the energy that large models use isn't free either.
  • It can wear down your own skills. If you stop checking its work, you slowly lose the ability to.
  • It concentrates power. A handful of companies own the largest models, and they decide what those models will and won't do.

These are serious problems. But look at them closely and most of them are problems of use: what we trust it with, what we check, what we send, and who we let make the rules. That's why I think the answer is to use AI well, not to refuse it.

It isn't nuclear, and it isn't genetics

#Link to this section: It isn't nuclear, and it isn't genetics

I often hear AI compared to nuclear weapons or genetic engineering. I think that comparison is wrong, and I think it does harm.

Splitting the atom gave us a weapon that can destroy a city in seconds. Editing the genes of living things can change them for good, and those changes can pass to every generation that follows. A single mistake with either can be permanent and enormous, and they deserve the strictest controls we have.

AI, as we actually use it today, is different in kind. It writes text, describes pictures, suggests code and answers questions. Its mistakes are real, but most of them are the kind a person can catch: a wrong fact, a clumsy sentence, a bug. We can check them, correct them, and switch the tool off.

That doesn't mean AI needs no rules. It needs good ones: honesty about what it is, respect for privacy, and people held responsible for what they publish and decide. But treating a writing assistant as if it were a warhead makes us afraid of the wrong things, and it pushes useful tools away from the people who need them most.

The fear of losing control

#Link to this section: The fear of losing control

The deepest fear about AI isn't about wrong facts. It's the fear that machines will start making our choices for us. But a tool has no will of its own. It only has the authority we hand to it, and we don't have to hand it any. Religious fears show this clearly. Many people of faith worry, in ways that deserve respect rather than mockery, that building a thinking machine is people trying to play God, or that we'll trust a machine's answer over our own conscience and treat it as a modern idol. Underneath those worries is a simple question: who is in charge of a human life? My answer is the same as theirs. People are. A machine can only become an idol if we choose to bow to it.

The business wars between the largest technology companies show the same thing from the other side. Some of the loudest warnings that AI might "take over" come from inside that race, and they're useful to the people making them: a frightening product sounds like a powerful one, and rules written in a panic tend to favour the few companies big enough to follow them. Meanwhile, the real loss of control looks far more ordinary: a feed designed to keep you scrolling, a recommendation built to make you buy, an "agent" that clicks "accept" on your behalf. That isn't a machine taking power. It's a company deciding how much of your choice to keep for itself. In both cases the answer is the same: keep the decision with the person.

What it means to a blind developer

#Link to this section: What it means to a blind developer

When I lost my sight, I lost the ability to glance. I can no longer look at a screenshot a colleague pastes into a chat, a chart in a report or a photo someone sends me. I can't skim a long page for the one paragraph I need. Everything reaches me one line at a time, through a screen reader, in the order someone else decided.

AI gives some of that back. It can describe an image that has no alt text. It can tell me what's on a screen that my screen reader announces as "Button. Button. Graphic." It can summarise a long document so I know where to start listening. It can explain an error buried in a wall of output, or describe a diagram that would otherwise be a blank space.

For a sighted person these are conveniences. For a blind person they're often the difference between doing the work and asking someone else to do it. Independence isn't a small thing.

Blind content creators gain in the same way. AI can suggest a first draft of alt text for a photo you took but can't see, check that your headings make sense, or turn your notes into a tidy article. You still decide what's true and what gets published. But you're no longer stuck at the first step.

The weaknesses matter more for us, too. A sighted person can glance at a photo and see that the AI got it wrong. I can't. That's exactly why I'm strict about how I use it.

How I use it, day to day

#Link to this section: How I use it, day to day

Opinions are cheap, so here's what AI actually does in my working week while I build SightPress.

Proofreading my writing. I can't see a typo. A screen reader reads "form" and "from" with equal confidence, and a missing word slips past the ear far more easily than the eye. So once I've written something, this article included, I ask an AI to proofread it: spelling, grammar, repeated words, sentences that run on, American spellings that have crept in. I ask it to keep my voice and to list every change, so I can listen to each one and accept or reject it. The ideas, the opinions and the final wording are mine. The AI is the second pair of eyes I no longer have.

Planning coding tasks. Before I write code for a new feature, I describe what I want and ask the AI to help me break it into steps: which parts of the system it touches, what could go wrong, what order to build things in, and what "done" looks like. A plan in plain text is far easier to read with a screen reader than dozens of open files. I argue with the plan, cut what I don't need and change what I disagree with before I start. Every stage of SightPress begins with a written plan like that, and the decisions in it are mine.

Writing automated tests. This is where AI helps me most. I can't glance at a page to see whether a change broke something, so I rely on tests to tell me, in words, what passed and what failed. I ask the AI to draft tests for the code I've written: the normal case, the edge cases, the errors, and checks that the admin panel's markup stays accessible. Then I read them and ask the awkward question: does this test check real behaviour, or does it just repeat the code back to itself? Unit tests must cover every line of SightPress's core code before a change is accepted, and AI makes that standard achievable for one person. The tests keep the AI honest too. When it suggests wrong code, a test usually catches it before I do.

The pattern is the same every time. The AI does the tiring, repetitive part. I review, decide and take responsibility.

The rules I use it by

#Link to this section: The rules I use it by

I don't think "be careful" is enough advice. Here's what I actually believe, and what I'd ask anyone using AI, in SightPress or anywhere else, to hold to.

  1. A person makes every decision. AI can suggest, draft and explain. It doesn't publish, send, buy or agree to anything on anyone's behalf. If a tool wants to act in your name, you should be able to see what it did and undo it.
  2. If you can't check it, don't publish it. Treat everything AI writes as a first draft from a confident stranger. Check facts against a real source. If you can't check something yourself, ask someone who can before it goes out.
  3. You're responsible, not the tool. "The AI wrote it" is never an excuse. Your name is on the page.
  4. Only share what's yours to share. Don't paste other people's personal details, private messages or confidential documents into an AI service unless you know where they go and you have the right to send them.
  5. Keep it optional and replaceable. Prefer tools you can switch off, swap for another provider or do without. No one should be forced to use AI to get a job done, and no one should be locked in to one company.
  6. Use it to do more, not to care less. AI should free your time for the thinking only you can do. If it's making you stop thinking, you're using it wrong.
  7. Don't use it to deceive. No fake reviews, no fake voices, no fake people. Be honest about where AI has helped when it matters to your readers.

And one more, aimed at the people who make the rules: refusing AI isn't automatically the safe or ethical choice. If a ban or a blanket "no AI" policy shuts blind and disabled people out of tools that give them independence, while everyone else carries on, that isn't caution. It's another barrier.

How SightPress puts this into practice

#Link to this section: How SightPress puts this into practice

These rules aren't just words in an article. They shape how the SightPress AI assistant works.

  • It's off unless you turn it on. New sites start without it. Every task in SightPress can be done without AI.
  • You choose the provider. An admin connects their own key from Anthropic, OpenAI or Mistral, or any service or self-hosted server that works like OpenAI's. Nothing is sent anywhere until they do. Keys are stored encrypted, and a monthly budget keeps costs under control.
  • It suggests; it never decides. Nothing the assistant writes is used until a person inserts it and saves. It never publishes anything on its own.
  • Unchecked AI work can't go live. AI-written alt text and translations stay marked until someone has checked them, and a page that uses them can't be published before then.

That's what using AI well looks like in practice: not blind trust and not blind fear, but a tool kept in human hands.

My view

#Link to this section: My view

I've lived through the whole history of the web, from the first static pages to today. I've seen every new technology called the end of something. Most of them turned out to be the beginning of something instead.

I'm not afraid of AI. I use it every day, and it has never made a decision for me, because I've never let it. What I am afraid of is the people who could gain most from it, blind people, disabled people and small organisations with no budget, being told it's too dangerous to touch while everyone else carries on using it.

AI won't save us and it won't destroy us. It will do what we ask of it, as well or as badly as we allow. So let's ask it to do good, check its work, and keep the decisions where they belong: with us.

Follow the development of SightPress on GitHub.

entry.title: SightPress 0.3.0: private analytics and an AI assistant that only suggests
entry.summary: SightPress 0.3.0 adds private analytics you can understand without seeing a chart, and an optional AI assistant that only suggests.
entry.content:
SightPress 0.3.0 is out, later on the same day as 0.2.0. It adds two features I've wanted from the start: analytics you can understand without seeing a chart, and an optional AI assistant that leaves every decision to you.

What's new

#Link to this section: What's new

Analytics without cookies

#Link to this section: Analytics without cookies

SightPress now counts visits, popular pages, sources, searches and bots on your own server. It uses no cookies or tracking scripts and sends nothing to other companies. It never stores visitors' IP addresses or browser details, and it doesn't count people whose browser asks not to be tracked.

Every chart comes with a summary in words, such as "Visitors went up 12% compared with the previous 30 days", and the same data in a table. Lines differ by shape as well as colour, and any table can be downloaded as a CSV file. Analytics is on by default, and an admin can turn it off for a site.

An optional AI assistant

#Link to this section: An optional AI assistant

The assistant is off for new sites. An admin can turn it on with their own key from Anthropic, OpenAI or Mistral, or connect any service or self-hosted server that works like OpenAI's. Keys are stored encrypted, and a monthly budget keeps costs under control.

Once it's on, the assistant can:

  • answer questions about using SightPress, pointing only to screens you can use
  • draft summaries, search descriptions, rewrites and whole pages
  • explain a publishing check
  • suggest image descriptions
  • draft translations that keep a page's blocks and links

A person always decides

#Link to this section: A person always decides

Nothing the assistant writes is used until a person inserts it and saves. AI-written alt text and translations stay marked until someone has checked them, and a page that uses them can't be published before then. AI can be a real help for a blind creator, but it can also be confidently wrong about a picture, so the final word stays with a person.

Clearer upload limits

#Link to this section: Clearer upload limits

SightPress now shows the largest file you can upload, warns admins about server settings that stop uploads, and explains what happened when a file is too large.

What it isn't yet

#Link to this section: What it isn't yet

SightPress is still an early release for trying out and testing, and running it on a public server isn't covered yet.

Try it

#Link to this section: Try it

The SightPress documentation includes guides to reading your analytics and setting up the assistant, and the 0.3.0 release notes list every change.

If you try the charts with a screen reader, or the image descriptions on your own pictures, please tell me what worked and what didn't.

entry.title: SightPress 0.2.0: languages, members and site search
entry.summary: SightPress 0.2.0 adds websites in several languages, member accounts and site search, to help you run a website over time.
entry.content:
SightPress 0.2.0 is out. The first release let you publish a website. This one helps you run it over time, in more than one language and for more than one kind of audience.

What's new

#Link to this section: What's new

Publish in several languages

#Link to this section: Publish in several languages

A site can now use any available language, and each page can have its own translation with its own title, address and content. Translations start as drafts, so nothing goes live by accident. Search engines are told which pages are translations of each other, and each language gets its own sitemap.

The admin panel, site texts and emails are now available in European Portuguese and Spanish as well as UK English.

Search every site

#Link to this section: Search every site

Every page now has a search form, with no outside service to pay for or configure. It ignores capitals and accents, so "cafe" finds "Café". Results show short extracts with your words marked in bold and underlined, so the match doesn't depend on colour.

Open a site to members

#Link to this section: Open a site to members

People can create their own account when a site allows it, confirming it with a six-digit code from an email. You can make single pages or a whole site readable only by signed-in members, and those pages stay out of search engines.

Change pages with confidence

#Link to this section: Change pages with confidence
  • Older versions: compare any version word by word. Changes are written out as "removed" and "added", so they read the same with a screen reader and without colour.
  • Safe restores: bringing back an older version never publishes it.
  • Scheduling: publish or unpublish a page at a set time.
  • Moving pages: copy, archive, trash and move pages, with redirects that keep old addresses working.

Choose your features

#Link to this section: Choose your features

Admins can turn optional features on or off for each site. Turning one off keeps its data, so turning it back on brings everything back as it was.

What it isn't yet

#Link to this section: What it isn't yet

SightPress is still an early release for trying out and testing, and running it on a public server isn't covered yet.

Try it

#Link to this section: Try it

The SightPress documentation has step-by-step guides, and the 0.2.0 release notes list every change.

If you can review the Portuguese or Spanish, or would like to help bring SightPress to another language, I'd love to hear from you.

entry.title: Why WordPress and other popular CMSs still fail blind and low-vision creators
entry.summary: Popular CMSs can build accessible websites, but few let a blind or low-vision person run one on their own. Here's why.
entry.content:
Nearly four in ten websites run on WordPress. Add Wix, Squarespace, Joomla, Drupal and the rest, and most of the web is built with a handful of content management systems. If you're blind or have low vision and you want to publish something, one of these is almost certainly what you'll be offered.

Most of them can produce an accessible website. Far fewer let a blind person build and run that website on their own. That gap is what this article is about.

Two sides of every CMS

#Link to this section: Two sides of every CMS

Every CMS has two faces. The public website is what visitors see. The admin panel is where someone writes the pages, uploads the images, fixes the menu and presses "Publish".

Most accessibility work in the CMS world goes into the public side, and that's understandable. That's where the law looks first, and it's where most people are. With a good theme, care and some expertise, WordPress, Drupal and the others can all produce pages that a screen reader user can read comfortably.

The admin panel gets much less attention. The unspoken assumption is that the person running the site can see it. For a blind charity worker, a partially sighted councillor or a small business owner losing their sight, that assumption decides whether they can do their job.

There's a standard for this side too, the Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG). It asks two things of a CMS: that its own interface is accessible, and that it helps authors produce accessible content. Hardly any mainstream CMS claims to meet it in full, and WordPress states that it does not currently conform.

Built for the eye first

#Link to this section: Built for the eye first

Modern editors are designed around looking. You see the page as it will appear, you drag a block where you want it, and you click a small icon to change it. For a sighted person this is quick and pleasant. With a screen reader it turns into a guessing game.

WordPress's block editor, Gutenberg, is the best-known example. Two months before it shipped in December 2018, the WordPress accessibility team lead, Rian Rietveld, resigned, citing political complications and new features that weren't keyboard tested before they were implemented. In 2019 WPCampus commissioned an independent accessibility audit of the editor, funded by community donations and Automattic. It found "significant and pervasive accessibility problems" (PDF, 1.6 MB), affecting blind, low-vision and motor-impaired users among others.

Things have improved since then, and the people working on WordPress accessibility deserve credit for that. But the editor's basic shape hasn't changed. It's still a visual canvas with floating toolbars, nested blocks and controls that appear and disappear depending on where your mouse or cursor is. To a screen reader user that means:

  • toolbars that only exist while a block is selected, so you have to know they're there before you can find them;
  • the same sort of block nested inside itself, with little to tell you which level you're on;
  • settings tucked into sidebars, popovers and "more options" menus behind icons, in an admin where missing labels were still being fixed in 2026;
  • moving content by drag and drop, with keyboard alternatives that are easy to miss or hard to use.

Hosted builders like Wix and Squarespace lean even harder on the visual canvas. Their editors are built around dragging things around a design. Wix has added an accessibility checker, which is welcome, but both editors are still tools you mostly operate with your eyes.

The plugin problem

#Link to this section: The plugin problem

Even when the core of a CMS is reasonably accessible, very few people use it on its own.

A typical WordPress site has a theme, a page builder, a forms plugin, an SEO plugin, a cookie banner, a gallery and a backup tool. Each comes from a different company, with its own screens, its own idea of a button and its own approach to accessibility, which is often none at all. Popular page builders replace the editor completely with an even more visual one.

So the question "Is WordPress accessible?" has no real answer. Your WordPress is a combination nobody has tested. One plugin update can put an unlabelled toggle on the screen you use every day, or a pop-up that takes your keyboard focus and never gives it back. Nothing in the system stops that happening, and nothing tells you it has.

Accessibility in these systems is something you can add. That also means it's something that can be left out.

Low vision is its own problem

#Link to this section: Low vision is its own problem

Blindness gets most of the attention, but many more people have low vision. They often use their remaining sight with magnification, high contrast or very large text, and different things break for them.

Admin panels are dense. They're full of small grey text, thin outlines and icons that only make sense at normal size. Zoom in to 300 or 400 percent and many of them fall apart. Sidebars cover the content, sticky toolbars hide the very text you're editing, and controls go off the edge of the screen. The media library, a grid of small thumbnails, is especially hard if you can only see part of the screen at once.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, the current web accessibility standard, added rules for exactly these problems. For example, it says that the thing you're working on must not be hidden behind sticky bars, and that every drag action needs a simple alternative. Many admin panels were designed long before those rules existed.

Retrofitting is the hardest way to do it

#Link to this section: Retrofitting is the hardest way to do it

None of this happens because the people behind these systems don't care. Many of them care a great deal. The problem is history.

WordPress started in 2003 as blogging software. Wix started as a visual site builder. Each decade added another layer: new editors, new frameworks, thousands of plugins and millions of sites that depend on all of it staying as it is. Making that admin panel truly accessible means redesigning its core interactions without breaking everything built on top. That's slow, expensive and politically difficult, so progress comes one bug fix at a time.

Retrofitting accessibility almost never catches up with the speed of new visual features. Every release adds new screens, and the accessibility work goes on chasing them.

What a blind creator actually needs

#Link to this section: What a blind creator actually needs

The needs aren't exotic. A blind or low-vision person running a website needs:

  • screens with real headings and landmarks, so they can jump around instead of listening to everything;
  • every control labelled with words, not just an icon;
  • everything possible with a keyboard, including reordering and moving content;
  • clear spoken feedback when something is saved, fails or changes;
  • layouts that still work at 400 percent zoom and in high-contrast modes;
  • an editor that helps them write accessible content, such as prompting for image descriptions and checking the heading outline;
  • the confidence that an add-on or update can't quietly take any of this away.

None of these is a nice-to-have. Each one decides whether a person can publish on their own or has to ask someone sighted for help.

Starting from the other end

#Link to this section: Starting from the other end

I'm a blind web developer, and this is why I'm building SightPress instead of filing more bug reports. SightPress is a CMS for everyone, designed with blind and low-vision creators and audiences in mind. It is built on modern object-oriented PHP and released as free software under the GPL. It starts from the admin panel, not the public website. Accessibility is a floor that themes and modules can't lower. Every change is tested automatically, and every milestone is checked by ear with real screen readers.

The popular systems will keep improving, and I hope they do. But "you can make it accessible if you know how and choose the right plugins" isn't good enough for people who can't see the screen. Publishing on the web should work for them from the moment they first sign in.

Follow the development of SightPress on GitHub.

entry.title: SightPress 0.1.0: the first usable version
entry.summary: SightPress 0.1.0 is out: the first version you can run on your own computer to create a website and publish pages.
entry.content:
Two weeks ago I announced a plan with no code to download. Today, SightPress 0.1.0 is out, and you can run it on your own computer, create a website and publish pages.

SightPress is a powerful content management system for everyone, designed with blind and low-vision creators and audiences in mind. It's free software, written in modern, object-oriented PHP.

What you can do

#Link to this section: What you can do

Build pages from blocks

#Link to this section: Build pages from blocks

There are ten block types: heading, text, image, gallery, video, audio, file download, columns, call to action and contact form. Pages move from draft through review to published.

Catch problems before publishing

#Link to this section: Catch problems before publishing

SightPress checks each page before it goes live, including its image descriptions, link text, captions, transcripts and heading order. Accessibility errors stop the page from being published until they're fixed, and search engine issues appear as warnings.

Work from an accessible admin panel

#Link to this section: Work from an accessible admin panel

The admin panel covers pages, media, menus, people, site settings and branding. Upload progress is announced, and the menu shows only what your role can use. An audit log records who changed what.

Sign in without risky links

#Link to this section: Sign in without risky links

Password resets and invitations use a six-digit code that you type on a page, never a link in an email. That's easier with a screen reader, and it gives people one less link to be tricked by.

Run several sites

#Link to this section: Run several sites

One installation can run several sites, each with its own people, pages and files. Each new site starts with ready-made pages and menus in the default theme, and SightPress checks that theme's colour contrast and base font size.

Be found by people, search engines and AI

#Link to this section: Be found by people, search engines and AI

Every public page has its own title, description and structured data, and is listed in a sitemap. It's also available as Markdown for AI tools, and each site decides how AI crawlers may use its content.

What it isn't yet

#Link to this section: What it isn't yet

This is an early release for trying out and testing. The admin panel is in UK English only, and running SightPress on a public server isn't covered yet.

Try it and tell me what breaks

#Link to this section: Try it and tell me what breaks

The SightPress documentation has a getting started guide for non-developers, and the 0.1.0 release notes list every change.

If you use a screen reader, a magnifier, a braille display, voice control or only a keyboard, I especially want to hear where SightPress gets in your way.

entry.title: Going blind as a web developer: what changed and what didn't
entry.summary: How losing my sight changed the way I write code, what stayed the same, and why it led me to build SightPress.
entry.content:
I was told I would go blind in 1995. It took almost thirty years to arrive. When it finally did, the tool that got me back to work was Windows Notepad.

A blank page and a voice

#Link to this section: A blank page and a voice

Notepad has no syntax highlighting, no panels, no tabs and no icons. For a sighted developer it feels like a punishment. In 2024 it was the first screen that made sense to me again: a blank page, a cursor, and a voice reading back each line I typed.

It was not elegant code, and it was not fast. But it was code, written by me, without seeing it. Some months earlier I had quietly decided my working life was over. Sitting in front of that old friend, the one we all used back when the web was new, I started to suspect I had been wrong.

What changed

#Link to this section: What changed

The diagnosis was retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic condition that narrows your sight slowly over many years. For most of my career it was background noise. Then, at the start of 2024, reading from a screen became very hard, and ordinary life became noticeably harder to manage with the sight I had left. Six months later I realised it was gone.

Reading in order

#Link to this section: Reading in order

The biggest change is that you can no longer glance. A sighted person looks at a screen and takes in its shape in a fraction of a second: where the menu is, where the error is, which part matters. A screen reader gives you none of that. Everything arrives one item at a time, in the order someone else decided, and you have to build the picture in your head.

My first weeks with screen readers were genuinely stressful. The narration was hard to follow, and working out where I was on a page felt like navigating a building by touch with the lights off. I had spent decades scanning code and interfaces. Now I had to listen to them.

What helps you is structure. Proper headings let you jump through a document instead of wading through it. Labels tell you what a control does before you press it. When they are there, a screen reader is fast. When they are missing, it is like reading a book with the chapter titles torn out and every sentence in the same voice.

Learning again, quickly

#Link to this section: Learning again, quickly

The second change surprised me: how quickly I adapted once I stopped waiting to feel ready. Notepad led to VS Code. VS Code led back to my favourite command-line tools, which turned out to be some of the most accessible software I own, because text in a terminal is just text.

Before long I was back alongside my colleagues at the insurance company where I still work, reviewing pull requests, fixing bugs and improving code. I'm proud of that, and I don't think I need to pretend otherwise.

What didn't change

#Link to this section: What didn't change

Here is the part that I didn't expect, and that people rarely believe at first: almost everything that made me a good engineer is still there.

I came up through web development from its early days to the present, through small agencies, telecoms and finance. Over those years I learned modern object-oriented programming, the SOLID principles, automated testing, and the discipline of CI/CD pipelines that won't let bad code through. None of that lived in my eyes.

My judgement about how a system should be shaped is the same. I still know when a class is doing too much, when an abstraction is hiding a problem instead of solving it, and when a quick fix will cost us later. My debugging instincts are the same: form a theory, test it, narrow it down. My taste for clean, well-named code is, if anything, stronger, because now I hear every badly named variable read aloud.

Code review works too. A diff is text. A failing test is text. A stack trace is text. Good tools present them in a sensible order, and I can work through them as well as I ever did.

So when I took stock, the conclusion was clear. The developer was fine. The tools were the problem.

Where the tools fail

#Link to this section: Where the tools fail

Code turned out to be the easy part. The web browser was the next challenge, and it was much harder.

Most of the sites I used to enjoy turned into a nightmare almost overnight. Social networks, which are mostly visual, I simply had to stop using. Reading Gmail in the browser became a slog. Even reading the news, something I had done every day of my adult life without thinking, became a fight with menus, pop-ups and unlabelled controls between me and the first paragraph.

Then I tried to do what so many people do on the web every day: create and edit content. That is where it stopped being an inconvenience and became a wall.

To a screen reader user, a typical content management admin screen sounds something like this: "Button. Button. Link. Graphic. Button. Button." Icons with no names. Toolbars you can only operate with a mouse. Drag-and-drop with no alternative. Dialogs that open without telling you, and leave you stranded somewhere behind them.

If you can see, you never notice any of this. If you can't, you can't publish. For most blind people I've spoken to, reading the web is hard, but adding to it is often impossible. That's a strange situation for a medium that was supposed to give everyone a voice.

Why I decided to build

#Link to this section: Why I decided to build

I could have written a long list of complaints and sent it to vendors. Plenty of people have, and plenty of those lists are still waiting for answers.

Instead I looked at what I had: decades of experience building for the web, a fresh and very personal understanding of where it fails, and the time and stubbornness to do something about it. So I decided to put my coding skills to work and build a new content management system from the ground up. Some weeks ago I started planning it: who it was for, what it had to do and what it must never do. It didn't even have a name yet.

The key word is "ground". I've learned that accessibility bolted on at the end never quite fits. It has to be the foundation, there from the first line of code, so that it can't be forgotten or switched off.

Beyond sight

#Link to this section: Beyond sight

The name came on 1 November 2026, the day I registered sightpress.org. The result is SightPress: a CMS for everyone, designed with blind and low-vision creators and audiences in mind. It is built on modern object-oriented PHP and released as free software under the GPL. It should be just as beautiful and easy to use for sighted people, because good accessible design is simply good design.

I want it to be the first choice for charities, public bodies, small businesses and individuals who care about accessibility. Our motto is "Beyond sight."

Notepad gave me a blank page and a voice that told me where I was. That isn't a high bar, and every tool that lets people publish on the web should clear it.

Follow the development of SightPress on GitHub.

entry.title: Introducing SightPress: a CMS for everyone, built from the ground up for accessibility
entry.summary: A blind web developer's plan for SightPress: a free, open-source CMS for everyone, built from the ground up for blind and low-vision creators.
entry.content:
I'm a blind web developer, and I can't comfortably run a website with most of the tools built for the job. For the past two months I have been planning something to fix that. On Sunday I registered its name.

SightPress is a powerful content management system for everyone, designed with blind and low-vision creators and audiences in mind. It will be written in modern, object-oriented PHP and released as free software under the GPL. Our motto is "Beyond sight."

There is no code to download yet. This article explains what I plan to build, why it should exist and what comes next.

The problem

#Link to this section: The problem

I lost my sight in 2024 to a genetic condition. With a screen reader, I went back to writing and reviewing code at work. Publishing on the web turned out to be much harder.

Many content management systems can produce a public website that a screen reader user can read. Far fewer let that same person build and run the website on their own. Their admin screens lean on small icons, drag and drop, floating toolbars and pop-ups that assume you can see what just changed.

That shuts out blind and low-vision people who want to write, and it causes problems for the organisations that employ them. A charity, a council or a small business can have an accessible website and still have an admin panel that one of its own staff can't use.

The idea

#Link to this section: The idea

SightPress starts from one rule: accessibility is the floor, quality design is the goal, and neither is ever traded for the other.

In practice, that means:

  • Accessibility can't be switched off, by a setting, a theme or an add-on.
  • Blind creators are treated as primary users of the admin panel, not as an edge case.
  • The product should be just as clear and attractive for people who can see it. Good structure, plain language and sensible defaults help everyone.

Major features

#Link to this section: Major features

An admin panel you can use without seeing it

#Link to this section: An admin panel you can use without seeing it

The admin panel will be rendered on the server, with very little JavaScript, because plain and predictable pages work better with screen readers. Every task will work with a keyboard alone. Fields will have labels, errors will link to the field that needs fixing, and status changes will be announced. Move up and move down buttons will replace drag and drop.

Every admin task will also have a documented command-line equivalent, for people who prefer a terminal and as a fallback if a screen ever lets someone down.

Publishing that helps you get it right

#Link to this section: Publishing that helps you get it right

Pages are built from blocks such as headings, text, images, video, audio, downloads and forms. Before a page goes live, SightPress will check its heading order, image descriptions, video captions, audio transcripts and link text. Accessibility errors will block publishing until they're fixed, and search engine issues will appear as warnings.

Pages will move through a clear workflow from draft to review to published, with scheduling, revisions and text-based comparisons that don't rely on colour. If a page moves, its old address will keep working through an automatic redirect.

Many sites and many languages

#Link to this section: Many sites and many languages

One installation will be able to run many sites. Each will have its own domains, database, file storage and users, so a group of charities or a web agency can keep them properly separate.

Every site can publish in any available language, including right-to-left languages and script variants such as Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin. The admin panel will start in UK English, followed by Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Hebrew and Arabic.

Themes that can't lower the floor

#Link to this section: Themes that can't lower the floor

A theme will be able to change colours, typography, spacing and components, with dark mode, increased contrast and reduced motion supported. SightPress will check colour contrast and refuse a theme that fails. A theme can restyle a site, but it can't remove its accessibility features.

Search and analytics, included

#Link to this section: Search and analytics, included

Every site will have an accessible search, with no outside service to pay for or configure.

The built-in analytics will use no cookies, tracking scripts or third parties. IP addresses won't be stored, and visitors can't be followed from one day to the next. Every chart will come with a plain-language summary and the same data in a table, so nobody needs to see a graph to understand how their site is doing. Site admins can turn either feature off.

An optional AI assistant that never decides for you

#Link to this section: An optional AI assistant that never decides for you

If a site admin turns it on and adds a key from their chosen provider, an assistant will help with admin questions and draft text, summaries, image descriptions and translations. Self-hosted models will be supported too.

Everything it writes is a suggestion. A person reviews it, and the assistant can never publish, send or delete anything by itself. SightPress will never hold or resell a key.

Found by people, search engines and AI

#Link to this section: Found by people, search engines and AI

Pages will have clean, semantic HTML, complete metadata, structured data and sitemaps. Each public page will also be available as Markdown for AI tools, and site owners will decide whether AI crawlers can read their content.

Open to extension

#Link to this section: Open to extension

Every feature, including the core ones, will be built as a module using the same public contract. A third-party module will be able to do what a built-in one can, while working within the same accessibility rules.

Why choose SightPress

#Link to this section: Why choose SightPress
  • Blind and low-vision creators can publish on their own, without asking a sighted colleague to finish the job.
  • Charities, public bodies and schools get a strong starting point for their accessibility duties, with WCAG 2.2 AA as the minimum target. No software can make an organisation compliant by itself, but the right tool can make it much easier to stay on track.
  • Small businesses and individuals get search, analytics, languages and accessible design without assembling a stack of plugins.
  • Readers get pages that work with screen readers, magnifiers, braille displays, voice control and keyboards.
  • PHP developers get a modern, strictly typed codebase with automated tests and a clear way to extend it.
  • Everyone keeps control of their data. SightPress won't send usage data back to the project, and the code will be open for anyone to inspect.

How it will be built

#Link to this section: How it will be built

I've learned the hard way that accessibility added at the end never quite fits, so the checks start with the first feature. Every change will go through automated tests and accessibility scans. Automated tools catch only part of the problem, so every milestone will also be tested by ear with real screen readers.

What comes next

#Link to this section: What comes next

Planning is nearly finished, and the build starts now. I'm working towards version 1.0 in these stages:

  1. Foundations: the code repositories, automated checks and module contract.
  2. First usable version: sites, users and roles, pages and blocks, the publishing workflow, the admin panel, a default theme and the full accessibility and search baseline.
  3. Content and languages: translations, page trees, members-only sites, site search, analytics and the AI assistant.
  4. Themes and media: installable themes, cloud storage, content delivery networks, captions and transcripts.
  5. Extensibility: third-party modules, custom roles and organisation-wide policies.
  6. Hardening: a security audit, privacy and GDPR tools, performance work, full documentation and a complete screen reader audit.
  7. Version 1.0: a stable public interface for developers and a documentation site.

After 1.0, the first planned add-on is a WordPress importer, so that moving an existing site doesn't mean starting again.

SightPress is based in the UK, so UK English and UK law come first. After that, I plan to roll out to the EU and its neighbouring countries, the Americas, Israel and then the rest of the world.

Come along

#Link to this section: Come along

I'd especially like to hear from blind and low-vision people who publish on the web, or who have given up trying. Tell me which tasks stop you. Testers, translators, designers, developers and organisations with real accessibility needs will all be welcome as the project grows.

You can find the project at sightpress.org, and the code will appear on the SightPress GitHub organisation as the work begins.

The web was supposed to give everyone a voice. I'm building SightPress so that more of us can use it.
